entries.topic: Ernest Bevin and British Palestine policy, July 1945 – 1946

claims.text: Clement Attlee formed his Labour government on 26 July 1945 and chose Ernest Bevin (born 9 March 1881, died 14 April 1951) as Foreign Secretary.
Britannica's only Palestine judgement on Bevin is that his plans of 1947–48 'for a federal Jewish-Arab nation or other partition of Palestine collapsed' in the face of the Arab-Israeli conflict.

On 13 November 1945 Bevin announced a 'joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship'; in the interim there would be 'no interruption of Jewish immigration at the present monthly rate' (no figure given in the text), and he spoke of a trusteeship agreement that would 'supersede the existing mandate'.
In the same statement Bevin referred to Palestinian Arabs' '90,000,000 co-religionists in India' and said Palestine 'does not by itself provide sufficient opportunity' for solving the Jewish problem.

The US Ambassador in London, John Winant, reported (telegram received 14 November 1945) that Bevin said he would be willing to 'stake his political future on finding solution for Palestine problem' and 'made a plea against approaching this subject in spirit of racial antagonism'.

According to Raphael Langham, Bevin told the Commons on 13 November 1945, 'We cannot accept the view that the Jews should be driven out of Europe', and at a press conference the same day warned that if Jews 'want to get too much at the head of the queue' there was a danger of antisemitic reaction; Langham calls the remark 'unfortunate'.

At the Labour Party conference in June 1946 Bevin said of American pressure to admit Jewish refugees to Palestine that 'They did not want too many Jews in New York'; Langham calls it 'a gratuitous sneer' that angered Truman and provoked protests in the United States.
At the Lancaster House (London) conference in September 1946, according to Langham, Bevin told the Arab delegation that no solution could ignore Jewish claims.
During his visit to the United States in November–December 1946, Bevin reportedly came to the view that Britain would have to give up the Mandate (Langham).

Langham records that a Foreign Office briefing attributed to Harold Beeley stressed Middle East oil, communications and the Suez route as Britain's interests, and cites W. Roger Louis on Britain's Middle East position.

Langham's own conclusion: Bevin was probably not motivated by antisemitism when he made policy and 'genuinely thought it was in the best interests of Britain', though his opposition hardened into anti-Zionism; Langham leaves open whether he then crossed into antisemitism.

disputes.question: What drove Bevin's opposition to a Jewish state?

positions.view: Personal hostility: contemporaries Christopher Mayhew ('Ernest detests Jews') and Chaim Weizmann ('blinded by his hatred of the Jews') said so; Peter Weiler finds he 'held antisemitic views' but 'no evidence that they shaped his policy'.
Anti-Zionist, not antisemitic: Alan Bullock (he 'was not moved by hatred of the Jews'), Ben-Gurion ('I prefer to consider Bevin simply as an anti-Zionist'), Attlee in the Commons in 1949.
Strategic interest: oil, communications and the Suez route, per the Foreign Office (Beeley) briefing and W. Roger Louis; Langham's own conclusion leans here.

claims.text: In early September 1945 Moshe Sneh and Yisrael Galili (Haganah), Natan Yellin-Mor (Lehi) and Menachem Begin (Irgun) agreed to form a united Jewish Resistance Movement; the Haganah acted through its Palmah.

Operations began on 1 November 1945 ('Night of the Trains'): at Lydda railway station Lehi and Irgun fighters destroyed three engines and damaged a train and a signal box, with some police and railway workers killed or injured.
The same night a Lehi bomb at the Haifa refinery went off early and killed the operation's commander, Moshe Bar-Giora; the heritage account calls the operation a failure.
On 17 June 1946 ('Night of the Bridges') the Palmah attacked eleven bridges across Palestine; the heritage account gives no casualty figure.

At the Jewish Agency's Paris meeting in early August 1946 the decision was taken to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met; the Congress in Basel decided on 9 December 1946 to halt the armed struggle, after which, in the Lehi account, the fight 'fell to Lehi and IZL'.
The Lehi heritage association's account is written from Lehi's own perspective; no casualty totals for the movement's operations are given in it.

sources.label: Lehi heritage site, 'The Jewish Resistance Movement: united armed offensive against the British'

entries.topic: Britain hands Palestine to the UN and decides to leave, February–September 1947 (with the Exodus and the sergeants)

claims.text: On 14 February 1947 Bevin told the Arab delegates that the Cabinet had agreed the question should go to the UN without British recommendations, 'inasmuch as plan offered by British Delegation had met with no acceptance from either Arabs or Jews'; Britain would present the matter 'as impartially as possible'.

In the Commons on 18 February 1947 Bevin described 'an irreconcilable conflict of principles': the Jews' essential principle was a sovereign Jewish state, the Arabs' was to resist Jewish sovereignty anywhere in Palestine; he called the Mandate 'unworkable in practice' and put the population at about 1,200,000 Arabs and 600,000 Jews (text as reproduced by the Center for Online Judaic Studies, without archival citation).
According to Langham, Bevin in the Commons blamed the Jews and the United States for the failure.

On 2 April 1947 Sir Alexander Cadogan for the UK asked the UN to 'place the question of Palestine on the Agenda of the General Assembly at its next regular Annual Session' and to 'summon, as soon as possible, a special Session' to constitute a special committee (document A/286, dated 3 April 1947).
The Exodus 1947 (formerly the President Warfield) sailed from Sète, France, in July 1947 with more than 4,500 Jewish passengers, mostly displaced persons and Holocaust survivors.
Three Jews (one crew member and two passengers, per USHMM) were killed and dozens wounded when the Royal Navy boarded the ship.

The passengers were transferred to three navy transports and taken back to Port-de-Bouc, France; France declined to remove them by force; after a hunger strike of 24 days and about three weeks in the summer heat, they were taken to Hamburg and interned in camps in the British zone of Germany.
Langham records that Bevin insisted the Exodus passengers be returned to their port of embarkation and suggests prejudice may have played a part.
Yad Vashem states the Exodus voyage was meant to draw the attention of UNSCOP members then working in the country; USHMM says the 'public embarrassment for Britain' helped shift diplomatic sympathy.

On 16 April 1947 Britain executed four Irgun members (Dov Gruner, Yehiel Dresner, Mordechai Alkahi, Eliezer Kashani); on 4 May 1947 the Irgun broke into Acre prison; three captured attackers (Avshalom Haviv, Yaakov Weiss, Meir Nakar) were sentenced to death and hanged on 29 July 1947.
The Irgun kidnapped Intelligence Corps Sergeants Clifford Martin and Mervyn Paice in Netanya on the night of 11–12 July 1947 and hanged them on 30 July 1947; the bodies were booby-trapped.
Anti-Jewish rioting broke out in Britain from 1 August 1947, beginning in Liverpool and spreading to other cities.
Arthur Creech Jones (Colonial Secretary in 1947) later (1961) listed the sergeants affair as one of four major factors behind the Cabinet's September 1947 decision to evacuate.

On 26 September 1947 Creech Jones told the UN Ad Hoc Committee that 'in the absence of a settlement' Britain had to plan for 'an early withdrawal of British forces and of the British administration', and that it 'was not prepared to undertake the task of imposing a policy in Palestine by force of arms'.

Britain abstained in the 29 November 1947 vote; in May 1948 Bevin told the Commons 'there are, after all, no Arabs in the House'; Britain recognised Israel in January 1949, with Bevin's acceptance 'grudging' (Langham).

disputes.question: Date and toll of the Exodus boarding

positions.view: Yad Vashem: attacked 17 July in international waters, three killed, reached Haifa 18 July.
USHMM: clash on 18 July 1947; one crew member and two passengers killed.

disputes.question: How much did the Jewish insurgency (and the sergeants affair) cause Britain's decision to leave?

positions.view: Decisive or near-decisive: J. Bowyer Bell called it the 'straw that broke the Mandate's back'; Creech Jones listed it among four major factors.
One factor among several: Britain's own stated reason was the irreconcilable Arab and Jewish positions and the failure of its own plan; Langham points to strategic and Arab-relations considerations.

entries.topic: UNSCOP: how the committee was formed, whom it heard, and how it voted (May–August 1947)

claims.text: The General Assembly's special session convened at Flushing Meadow on 28 April 1947 and on 15 May 1947 adopted Resolution 106 (S-1) creating the Special Committee on Palestine with 'the widest powers to ascertain and record facts', reporting by 1 September 1947.
Australia's proposal that the committee have eleven members, excluding the Security Council's permanent members, was adopted 13 to 11 with 29 abstentions.

Members: Australia, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, India, Iran, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden, Uruguay and Yugoslavia. Justice Emil Sandström (Sweden) was elected chairman on 2 June 1947, Alberto Ulloa (Peru) vice-chairman; the first meeting was at Lake Success on 26 May 1947.
Members arrived in Palestine on 14–15 June 1947 and first met in Jerusalem on 16 June 1947.

The Arab Higher Committee informed the Secretary-General on 13 June 1947 that it would abstain from cooperating; on 10 July 1947 its vice-chairman Jamal Husseini wrote that it would not reverse that decision.

The committee heard the governments of Egypt, Iraq, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Yemen in Beirut (22 July 1947, with Lebanese Foreign Minister Hamid Frangié), after an informal visit to Damascus on 21 July; Transjordan declined to send a representative outside the country, and the chairman and seven members visited King Abdullah in Amman on 25 July 1947.
For the Jewish Agency the committee heard Moshe Shertok and David Horowitz, and Chaim Weizmann in a personal capacity.
After a 6–4 vote with one abstention, a subcommittee visited displaced-persons camps (Munich, Salzburg, Vienna, Berlin, Hamburg, Hanover) on 8–14 August 1947.

The report was drafted in Geneva from 28 July; eleven recommendations were approved unanimously on 29 August and a twelfth with two dissents; the report was signed on 31 August 1947 (cover dated 3 September 1947).

The majority plan (partition with economic union, an international regime for Jerusalem) was backed by Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden and Uruguay; the minority plan (a federal state with Jerusalem as capital) by India, Iran and Yugoslavia; Australia abstained on both votes (7–3 and 3–7).
The Center for Israel Education states that eight of the eleven members endorsed partition and that the Jewish Agency accepted the plan, while the Arab Higher Committee rejected it.

disputes.question: Was the Arab case heard at all?

positions.view: The Palestinian Arab leadership (Arab Higher Committee) boycotted the committee, so no Palestinian Arab body testified.

The governments of six Arab states did present their case to the committee in Beirut, and members met King Abdullah in Amman; 'one side only' is accurate for Palestinian bodies, not for the Arab case as a whole.
Seven, with Australia abstaining (the committee's own report).
Eight of eleven (Center for Israel Education summary).

sources.label: Yearbook of the United Nations 1947–48, excerpts (UNISPAL)

entries.topic: Resolution 181: the votes, the timetable, and the contested numbers

claims.text: In the Ad Hoc Committee on 25 November 1947 the partition plan was adopted 25 to 13 with 17 abstentions; the draft for a unitary state (Draft Resolution III) was rejected 29 to 12 with 14 abstentions.
A Pakistani amendment to cap land ownership at 10% per group was rejected 22 to 8.

On 29 November 1947 the Assembly adopted the plan 33 to 13 with 10 abstentions. Abstaining: Argentina, Chile, China, Colombia, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Honduras, Mexico, the United Kingdom, Yugoslavia. Voting against: Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Greece, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey, Yemen. Those in favour included Australia, Canada, France, Poland, Sweden, the USSR, the United States and Uruguay.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen denounced the plan as contrary to the Charter, illegal and immoral, said they regarded it as a recommendation and would not feel bound by it.

The resolution set a timetable: the Mandate to end 'as soon as possible but in any case not later than 1 August 1948'; an area with a seaport in the Jewish state to be evacuated 'not later than 1 February 1948'; provisional councils of government by 1 April 1948; the two states to come into existence two months after evacuation and 'not later than 1 October 1948'. A five-member Palestine Commission (Bolivia, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Panama, the Philippines) was to carry it out.

The Jewish Agency's argument, as recorded in the Yearbook: the Arab states held about 17,000,000 Arabs in roughly 1,290,000 square miles; Palestine after Transjordan's separation was about 10,000 square miles; the plan made the Jewish National Home less than one-eighth of the territory originally set aside.

Muhsin Yusuf (Birzeit University) gives the proposed Jewish state about 498,000 Jews and about 494,000 Arabs, the Arab state about 725,000 Arabs and 11,000 Jews, and the Jerusalem district about 105,000 Arabs and 100,000 Jews; the Jewish state 56% of the land and the Arab state 43%; Jews owned about 10% of the Jewish state's land and about 6% of Palestine overall.

The Jewish Virtual Library, citing Howard Sachar, gives the Jewish state about 5,500 square miles with 538,000 Jews and 397,000 Arabs, and the Arab state 4,500 square miles with 804,000 Arabs and 10,000 Jews; citing Aharon Cohen, it says about 60% of the Jewish state was Negev desert.

Yusuf sets out the Arab reasons for rejection as he reads them: fear of later expulsion and land confiscation, the injustice of granting statehood to a largely immigrant minority while the majority was denied self-determination, and a view of Zionism as a European imperial project; he cites the Arab case to the 1946 Anglo-American Committee that Jews 'will be full citizens' of a Palestinian state.

The Jewish Virtual Library states that the Jews of Palestine were dissatisfied with the territory and with Jerusalem's separation but 'welcomed the compromise'; it reports Arab League Secretary-General Azzam Pasha telling David Horowitz and Abba Eban on 16 September 1947 that 'The Arab world is not in a compromising mood' (citing Avneri and Horowitz).

disputes.question: Population of the proposed Jewish state

positions.view: About 498,000 Jews and 494,000 Arabs — a near-even split (Yusuf, Palestine-Israel Journal, 2002).
538,000 Jews and 397,000 Arabs (Sachar, cited by the Jewish Virtual Library).

disputes.question: Share of the land allotted to the Jewish state

positions.view: 56% (Yusuf).
About 5,500 of roughly 10,000 square miles, about 60% of it Negev desert (JVL citing Sachar and Cohen).

entries.topic: Palestinian Arab leadership and the Arab League, 1945–1948

claims.text: From its founding in March 1945 until Britain's withdrawal decision in autumn 1947 the Arab League consistently supported a 'unitary and independent Palestinian state' (Shlaim).
The Arab Higher Committee was re-established in 1946, after a nine-year hiatus, not by the Palestinian parties as in 1936 but 'by a decision of the Arab League' (Shlaim).

Arab League Council decisions as listed by the Jewish Virtual Library from League records: December 1945, a committee to enforce the boycott of Zionist goods (Res. 16) and up to three Palestinian representatives on the Council (Res. 17); March 1946, a £E1 million company to buy Arab land in Palestine; June 1946 at Bludan, the boycott made part of the 'creed of the Arab nations', a call to make land sales to Zionists a crime (Res. 72), and a Higher Arab Executive for Palestine (Res. 80, 82); December 1946, rejection of partition (Res. 142); October 1947 at Aley, 'Defending Palestine' (Res. 181) calling for military preparations along Arab borders.

For the Cairo session of December 1947 the list records no public announcement and a decision against formal military intervention unless the United States and Britain intervened militarily; in February 1948 the Council approved political, military and economic measures, including withholding petroleum concessions and sanctions on states aiding the Zionists.

After the war Hajj Amin al-Husayni was refused asylum in Switzerland and held by France, which refused a British proposal to deport him to the Seychelles; in May 1946 he escaped from his residence near Paris to Cairo, where King Faruq gave him asylum, and the Arab League made him chairman of the new Arab Higher Committee.

At the League Council in Aley (October 1947) and Cairo (December 1947) the Mufti 'pleaded passionately for the establishment of a shadow government' under the Arab Higher Committee; in February 1948 the League rejected his demand for a government-in-exile and refused a loan for the Committee's administrative costs.
On 8 July 1948 the League's Political Committee agreed on a 'temporary civil administration' responsible to the League.

The All-Palestine Government was announced by the League's Political Committee at Alexandria on 20 September 1948 with its seat in Gaza; the Arab Higher Committee proclaimed Palestine independent on 22 September; a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza on 30 September 1948 under the Mufti's chairmanship; the government was headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi.

Egypt recognized the All-Palestine Government first, in mid-October 1948, followed by Iraq and then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia; Britain refused; Abdullah opposed it and said it would not operate in areas held by the Arab Legion.

On 1 December 1948 a congress of about 3,000 delegates in Jericho proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king; Abdullah afterwards stripped al-Husayni of the title of Mufti of Jerusalem.

The Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict describes the 1946 Arab Higher Committee as ineffective, with uncoordinated paramilitary forces, and the League as divided: Abdullah 'opposed every move toward Palestinian independence' and refused to deal with al-Husayni.

disputes.question: Who spoke for the Palestinian Arabs in 1947–48?

positions.view: The Arab League controlled the Palestinian leadership's instruments — it reconstituted the AHC, refused it a government-in-exile until September 1948, and armed the Arab Liberation Army under its own command (Shlaim).

The Mufti and the Arab Higher Committee pursued their own line — boycotting UNSCOP, pressing for a shadow government, forming the Army of the Holy War — but were weak and divided (Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict).

entries.topic: The civil war after the vote: irregulars, volunteer armies and the Jerusalem road (Dec 1947 – May 1948)

claims.text: The State Department's Office of the Historian describes the fighting after the partition vote as irregular Palestinian Arab bands, attached to Arab Liberation Army units, attacking Jewish cities, settlements and forces, with the Haganah, Irgun and Lehi fighting back.
The Arab Liberation Army was created by the Arab League and led by Fawzi al-Qawuqji; its forces were volunteers, 'few in number, and poorly armed' (Pogońska-Pol, 2019).

The Army of the Holy War (Jaysh al-Jihad al-Muqaddas) was made up of Palestinian volunteers and subordinate to the Husayni family; it and the Arab Liberation Army acted without cooperating, and neither stopped the Jewish forces (Pogońska-Pol).

Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni re-entered Palestine via the Egyptian border in December 1947 and, after the Arab Higher Committee proclaimed jihad, re-formed and commanded the Army of the Holy War; his explosives unit blew up the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem (no date given in the source).

At the end of March 1948 he went to Damascus seeking arms from the Arab League's Military Committee; Jewish forces took al-Qastal, overlooking the Jerusalem–Jaffa road, and he was killed on 8 April 1948 leading the counter-attack.
Before the Mandate ended the Arab Legion attacked the Gush Etzion bloc; its defenders surrendered and some were massacred (Shlaim's seminar notes).

entries.topic: The American retreat from partition: the trusteeship proposal of March 1948

claims.text: On 19 March 1948 Ambassador Warren Austin told the Security Council that the partition plan 'cannot now be implemented by peaceful means' and that 'a temporary trusteeship for Palestine should be established under the Trusteeship Council'.

Austin asked the Council to request a special session of the General Assembly under Article 20 and to instruct the Palestine Commission to 'suspend its efforts to implement the proposed partition plan'.
UN Secretary-General Trygve Lie, per his memoir as footnoted in FRUS, saw the new US position as 'a rebuff to the United Nations' and suggested that he and Austin resign; Austin declined.
A US memorandum records that Arab representatives 'were pleased with this latest turn of events, but they did not gloat'.

Abba Hillel Silver, for the Jewish Agency, told the Security Council on 19 March 1948 that the US proposal was 'a shocking reversal of its position', likely 'to lead to increased violence in Palestine'.

On 20 March 1948 Ben-Gurion declared: 'We shall not agree to any kind of trusteeship, whether permanent or temporary, even for the shortest time', calling the reversal 'a surrender to the terrorism of the Arab gangs' that would not 'prevent the establishment of the Jewish State'.

entries.topic: Plan Dalet: the text and the operations of April–May 1948

claims.text: Walid Khalidi's 'Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine' was republished in the Journal of Palestine Studies 18:1 (Autumn 1988) with the text of Plan D, dated 10 March 1948, as an appendix; Khalidi notes Plan D was 'finalized on 10 March 1948' and its operational objectives were put into practice from 1 April 1948.

The plan's text states: 'The objective of this plan is to gain control of the areas of the Hebrew state and defend its borders', including 'areas of Jewish settlement and concentration which are located outside the borders'.

Section 4(b) provides for 'Destruction of villages (setting fire to, blowing up, and planting mines in the debris)' and, where resistance is met, that 'the population must be expelled outside the borders of the state'.
Khalidi dates the earlier Plan B to September 1945 and Plan C (Gimmel) to May 1946, which he says was put into practice from 1 December 1947.

Khalidi's list of operations under Plan D (dates and outcomes as he gives them): Nachshon, 1 April (corridor Tel Aviv–Jerusalem; he marks it defeated); Harel, 15 April; Misparayim, 21 April (Haifa); Chametz, 27 April (villages around Jaffa); Jevussi, 27 April (Jerusalem); Yiftach, 28 April (eastern Galilee); Matateh, 3 May (Tiberias area); Maccabi, 7 May (Latrun); Gideon, 11 May (Beisan); Barak, 12 May (near Bureir); Ben Ami, 14 May (Acre); Pitchfork and Schfifon, 14 May (Jerusalem's New and Old City).
Khalidi writes that 'Up to 1 March not one single Arab village had been vacated by its inhabitants'; a footnote corrects this to note that at least ten villages had been captured by 1 March 1948.

Khalidi argues that Plan D created 'the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based', that the exodus was its product, and that the claim of Arab evacuation orders was 'a piece of mythmaking', citing BBC and FBIS monitoring; he faults Benny Morris for treating the exodus in 'an historical vacuum'.

positions.view: A master plan for conquest whose village clauses produced the exodus by design (Khalidi).

A military plan whose village clauses left expulsion to local commanders' discretion (Morris's reading, set out in the chapter's own Plan Dalet material); Khalidi's operation objectives are his own translations and characterizations.

sources.label: Walid Khalidi, 'Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine', Journal of Palestine Studies 18:1 (1988), with Plan D text (Appendix B)

entries.topic: Tiberias and Haifa, April 1948, and the dispute over why their Arab populations left

claims.text: Khalidi writes that the Zionist forces 'did not begin to seize and hold on to Arab territory' until the offensive that began on 1 April 1948.
Tiberias fell on 18 April 1948 and its Arab population (about 4,500–5,000, swollen by refugees from nearby villages) was evacuated.

In Haifa the Haganah's Carmeli Brigade under Moshe Carmel attacked early on 21 April 1948 as British forces withdrew from the dividing positions; Major-General Hugh Stockwell had told Arab representatives that day that his forces would redeploy; the city fell on 22 April.
Khalidi argues the Haganah had advance knowledge of the British redeployment and calls Stockwell 'an accomplice in the fall of Haifa'; he says the operation planned as Misparayim was renamed Chametz.

British figures cited by Khalidi put casualties at about 100 Arabs killed and 200 wounded, and about 20 Jews killed and 40 wounded; about 50,000 Arabs were crowded into the Old Town on 22 April, and Khalidi writes that 'Within a week, some 50,000 Arab inhabitants had been expelled'.

At the Town Hall on 22 April Stockwell warned the Arab delegates that if they did not sign the truce he would not be responsible if 'three or four hundred more' were killed; the delegates had no reply from Damascus, and, per the account of Koussa cited by Khalidi, their request for transport out was made 'on the spur of the moment', not under orders from Arab states.

An opinion article in the Jewish Chronicle (Florit Shoihet, 12 August 2026) reports that Haifa's mayor Shabtai Levy pleaded at the same meeting, 'Stay in the city and be equal citizens', that Stockwell told the delegates 'You have made a foolish decision', that the Haganah broadcast assurances of safety and civil rights, and that about 60,000 Arabs left; it cites no specific archive.

positions.view: Expelled by military attack and psychological warfare after British collusion; the evacuation request was improvised, not ordered by Arab states (Walid Khalidi, 1959/2008).

The Arab delegation chose evacuation over terms offering equal citizenship, despite pleas from the Jewish mayor and the British commander (Jewish Chronicle opinion, 2026, without archival references).
Khalidi records that Benny Morris first acknowledged the absence of Arab evacuation orders (1987) and later argued orders were issued after the fighting; Khalidi disputes the later position.

sources.label: Walid Khalidi, 'The Fall of Haifa Revisited', Journal of Palestine Studies 37:3 (2008), reprinting his 1959 article
Florit Shoihet, Jewish Chronicle opinion, 12 Aug 2026

entries.topic: Abdullah, the Jewish Agency and Britain, November 1947 – May 1948

claims.text: In early November 1947 at Naharayim, on the Jordan, Abdullah told Golda Meyerson (Meir) he intended to annex the Arab areas of Palestine; she replied that the Zionist leaders would not oppose this if there were no clashes between Jewish and Transjordanian forces.
Shlaim's seminar notes call the November 1947 understanding a 'tacit agreement'.

After a February 1948 meeting of the British Foreign Secretary, the Jordanian prime minister and Glubb, Glubb 'actively sought to thwart the efforts of the Arab irregular forces' and sought a military accord with the Zionists; Graham Jevon's study (Cambridge, 2017) says its findings corroborate Avi Shlaim's disputed claim that Britain gave Abdullah a 'green light' to occupy the areas allotted to the Arab state, and that Glubb was not the architect of the Greater Transjordan scheme but implemented it.
Shlaim writes that Britain 'was resigned to the emergence of a Jewish state but supported her client, King Abdullah', and 'helped to abort the birth of a Palestinian state'.

On 30 April 1948 the Arab League's Political Committee decided that 'all the Arab states must prepare their armies for the invasion of Palestine on 15 May'; under pressure from Transjordan and Iraq, Abdullah was named commander-in-chief.

On 10 May 1948 Meyerson and Ezra Danin crossed to Amman disguised as an Arab couple; Abdullah said he was now 'one of five' and asked, 'why don't you wait a few years? Drop your demands for free immigration.'

Per Meyerson's contemporary report (Shlaim's notes), Abdullah did not deny the earlier understanding, said he had no choice but to join the invasion, and they did not part as enemies; Yaacov Shimoni judged on 13 May that the king 'has not entirely betrayed the agreement, nor is he entirely loyal to it'.
Anti-Hashemite League states suspected Abdullah of collaborating with the Zionists; on 15 May Syrian President Shukri al-Quwwatli urged a halt to the advance and Abdullah refused (Shlaim's notes).

positions.view: Yes in substance: a tacit Abdullah–Jewish Agency understanding to divide the Arab state's territory, with a British 'green light' (Shlaim; corroborated by Jevon on the British side).

Partial at best: Abdullah joined the invasion as 'one of five' and asked the Jews to defer statehood; the Jewish Agency's own Shimoni judged him neither loyal to nor in full breach of the understanding.

entries.topic: The Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel, 14 May 1948

claims.text: The Declaration was read and signed in Tel Aviv on Friday 14 May 1948, at the Tel Aviv Museum ('on this Sabbath eve'); the text as reproduced carries both '5th day of Iyar, 5708 – 14th May 1948' in its signing line and '6th Iyar, 5708 (15th May, 1948)' in its body for the end of the Mandate.
It grounds the state on 'our natural and historic right', the Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917, the Mandate of the League of Nations, and the General Assembly resolution of 29 November 1947.
It promises equality of social and political rights 'irrespective of religion, race or sex'.

It appeals to the Arab inhabitants of the state 'to preserve peace' and participate on the basis of 'full and equal citizenship', and extends 'an offer of peace and good neighbourliness' to neighbouring states.
It makes the People's Council the Provisional Council of State, with a constitution to be adopted by an elected Constituent Assembly 'not later than the 1st October 1948'.
It states no borders; it refers to Eretz-Israel and pledges steps toward 'the economic union of the whole of Eretz-Israel'.

sources.label: Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel, text via Israel MFA (Jewish Virtual Library)

entries.topic: The Arab states' invasion and the war, 15 May 1948 – 1949

claims.text: In a cablegram of 15 May 1948 (S/745) the Secretary-General of the Arab League told the UN the Arab states were intervening 'to restore law and order and to prevent disturbances prevailing in Palestine from spreading' into their territories, now that the Mandate had ended 'leaving no legally constituted authority behind'.

The cablegram stated that 'approximately over a quarter of a million of the Arab population have been compelled to leave their homes' and backed 'the creation of United State of Palestine based upon the democratic principles'.

The Office of the Historian records an Arab air attack on Tel Aviv on the eve of 14 May; armies from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Egypt invaded, a Saudi formation fought under Egyptian command, and Transjordanian forces intervened only in areas designated for the Arab state or the Jerusalem corpus separatum; the US kept an arms embargo on all belligerents.
Shlaim gives the forces on 15 May 1948 as 35,000 Israeli troops against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops, and argues that 'illicit arms-imports decisively tipped the military balance in favour of Israel'.

Shlaim's seminar notes on the first round (15 May – 11 June): the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem surrendered on 28 May; three frontal attacks on Latrun (25 and 30 May, 9 June) were repelled by the Arab Legion; the Egyptian advance stalled at Ramat Rahel (24 May) and Ashdod (29 May); the Syrians were stopped at Degania but held Mishmar Hayarden; the Iraqis held the Jenin–Nablus–Tulkarem triangle.

The same notes say the forces Arab states actually sent were 'well below the level demanded by the Military Committee of the Arab League', that the Israeli army had more men but weaker firepower, and that the June truce was 'a turning-point'.

The first truce ran 28 days, from 11 June to 9 July 1948, supervised by the UN mediator Count Folke Bernadotte (appointed 21 May) with observers from Belgium, France, Sweden and the United States; materiel reached the Israeli army from Europe, 'particularly Czechoslovakia'; Bernadotte's proposal (the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs, Jerusalem under the UN) was rejected by both sides (IDF account via the Jewish Virtual Library).

The second truce began on 18 July 1948 at 19:00; the Arab Legion continued shelling West Jerusalem through October and demolished the UN-held Latrun pumping station on 12 August; a 'sincere cease-fire' in Jerusalem was agreed on 30 November (IDF account).

Operation Dani was launched from Ben Shemen on the night of 9–10 July 1948; the assault on Lydda began on 11 July and the town was under full control on 12 July without formal surrender; between 80 and 176 people were killed at the Dahmash mosque and more than 400 in the town (Sana Hammoudi, Palquest).

Citing Benny Morris, both Palquest and Zachary Lockman report that on 12 July Ben-Gurion answered a question about the inhabitants with 'Expel them'; Yitzhak Rabin then signed an order to expel Lydda's inhabitants quickly; Israeli censors made Rabin remove the episode from his memoir.

Lockman puts the combined population of Lydda and Ramla at 50,000–70,000, about 15,000 of them refugees, with 250–400 Palestinian civilians and four Israeli soldiers killed; Palquest estimates about 70,000 forced out on 13 July and close to 1,000 dead in the towns and on the march.

Israel signed separate armistice agreements in 1949 with Egypt, Lebanon, Transjordan and Syria; Egypt kept the Gaza Strip and Jordan the West Bank (Office of the Historian, which dates them 'February 1949').
More than 6,000 Israelis were killed in the war, about 1% of the roughly 650,000 Jews then in the country (Reuters, via Ynet, 2005).

positions.view: Israel 35,000 against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops (Shlaim).
Israel had more men but weaker firepower; Arab contingents fell short of the League's own requirement (Shlaim's notes) — compare the chapter's own July 1948 US assessment of about 90,000.

disputes.question: Lydda and Ramla: how many were expelled and killed

positions.view: About 70,000 expelled; more than 400 killed in Lydda; close to 1,000 dead including the march (Palquest).
Combined population 50,000–70,000; 250–400 civilians killed (Lockman, summarizing Morris).

entries.topic: The Palestinian refugees of 1948: how many, how they left, and the decision against return

claims.text: The UN Conciliation Commission's Technical Committee (report dated Lausanne, 19 August 1949, A/AC.25/Com.Tech/9) adopted an estimate by P. J. Loftus of the UN Statistical Office of about 711,000 refugees from Israeli-controlled territory, 'as accurate as circumstances permit'.
The same report noted that relief recipients outnumbered refugees because of duplicate ration cards, people displaced from other areas and destitute non-refugees.

Rex Brynen's Palestinian Refugee ResearchNet (McGill, 1996) gives the Conciliation Commission's figure as 726,000, UNRWA's 1950 figure as 957,000, the Israeli government's past figure as 'as low as 520,000' and Palestinian researchers' upper estimate as 850,000; about a third went to the West Bank, a third to Gaza, and the rest to Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and beyond.

According to Lockman's summary of Morris, an IDF intelligence report of June 1948 estimated that about 240,000 Arabs had fled the Jewish state's areas and about 150,000 other areas by 1 June 1948, attributing about 70% to direct Jewish military operations, 2% to psychological warfare and 2% to expulsion orders (Morris considers this an underestimate), and no more than 5% to Arab leaders' evacuation orders.
Morris concludes, per Lockman, that from June 1948 deliberate expulsions helped create about 300,000 further refugees but that there was no explicit, general Israeli decision to expel.

'As early as June 1948,' Lockman writes, 'the cabinet had reached a consensus against allowing the refugees to return to their homes'; he says Yosef Weitz's October 1948 report falsely blamed Arab leaders for organizing the flight.

Counts of depopulated villages differ by method: Benny Morris (1987) 369; Walid Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) 418, excluding towns and 151 places found on other lists; Aref al-Aref 399; Nijm and Muammer 443; Saleh 472; the Palestine Land Society 531 localities, counting tribal lands and towns.

Shlaim writes that Morris 'rejected both the "Arab order" and the "Jewish robber-state" explanations' and treated the refugee problem as 'a by-product of the war', while Shlaim holds that the evidence 'suggests a far higher degree of Israeli responsibility'.

disputes.question: How many Palestinians became refugees in 1947–49?

positions.view: About 711,000 (UN Conciliation Commission's technical estimate, 1949); PRRN cites the Commission at 726,000.
As low as 520,000 (past Israeli government figure).
Up to 850,000 (Palestinian researchers); 957,000 on UNRWA's 1950 rolls, which the 1949 report warned were inflated.
Mainly direct military action, with expulsions growing from June 1948; no general expulsion order; Arab evacuation orders marginal (Morris, as summarized by Lockman).
By design, under Plan Dalet (Khalidi), or with far higher Israeli responsibility than Morris allows (Shlaim).

entries.topic: Jews in Arab countries after the partition vote, 1947–1948

claims.text: On 30 November 1947, the day after the vote, riots against Jews broke out in Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo, Beirut and Aden; leaders of al-Azhar in Cairo declared a holy war against the Zionists (Center for Israel Education).

In Aleppo a mob broke into the Great Synagogue, destroying Torah scrolls and damaging the Aleppo Codex (most of it saved and smuggled to Jerusalem in 1958); 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues were destroyed.
In Bahrain on 5 December 1947 Jewish homes and shops were looted, the synagogue destroyed and one Jewish woman killed.

In Aden, a British colony, the riots that began on 2 December 1947 killed 82 Jews and wounded 76 (CIE); the Jewish Virtual Library gives 76–82 Jews and 38 others (33 Arabs, 4 Indian Muslims, one Somali) killed, with 106 of 170 Jewish-owned shops in Crater looted; a 1951 study gives 76 killed and 78 wounded.

In Egypt more than 1,000 Jews were arrested in Cairo on 15 May 1948; Proclamation No. 26 (29 May 1948) sequestered the property of internees (67 of 68 orders to 30 September involved Jews) and Proclamation No. 30 (6 June 1948) allowed warrantless searches of Jews (H. Dewey Anderson's 1951 study for the UN General Assembly).

Bombings in Cairo's Jewish quarters in 1948: on 20 June (Anderson: 12 houses, 20 killed; Wikipedia, citing Beinin: 22 killed, 41 wounded in the Karaite quarter); the Cicurel department store on 19 July; 22 September (19 killed). In November 1948 the government arrested 32 Muslim Brotherhood leaders and banned the group, and in a 1950 trial Brotherhood members were charged with the bombings of June–November.

Iraq's July 1948 law made Zionist activity punishable by death or at least seven years' imprisonment; Shafiq Ades was hanged on 23 September 1948; Jews were barred from banking and foreign-currency dealing (28 August 1948) and ordered discharged from government departments (19 October 1948).

Anderson's study also records 250 Jews imprisoned in Aleppo on 15 May 1948, a 'second wave of violence' in Tripoli, Libya, on 14 June 1948, and Yemen's ruler permitting the exit of its Jews in December 1948 (45,009 evacuated in what became known as 'Magic Carpet').

positions.view: 82 Jews killed, 76 wounded (Center for Israel Education; Jewish Virtual Library 76–82).
76 killed, 78 wounded (Anderson, 1951).

disputes.question: Death toll of the 20 June 1948 Cairo bombing

positions.view: 20 killed (Anderson, 1951).
22 killed, 41 wounded (Wikipedia, citing Beinin).

entries.topic: Jewish dissent in 1948: Arendt, Magnes and the Einstein letter

claims.text: Hannah Arendt's 'To Save the Jewish Homeland: There Is Still Time' appeared in Commentary in May 1948, pp. 398–406.

In Robert Manne's account, Arendt argued that Jewish near-unanimity for a state before any Arab-Jewish settlement would bring war, and that even a victorious Jewish state would remain small, surrounded by hostile neighbours and absorbed in self-defence.

She proposed a gradual binational federation built on mixed Jewish-Arab local councils under UN trusteeship with US and British support, writing, 'It is still not too late'; she condemned the Irgun's attacks, including Deir Yassin (Manne).
Judah Magnes, with whom Arendt worked closely, met Truman in May 1948 to press for a federation under trusteeship; in 1952 Arendt called Magnes 'the conscience of the Jewish people' (Manne).

A letter dated 2 December 1948 and published in the New York Times on 4 December 1948, signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook, protested Menachem Begin's US visit and described his Tnuat Haherut (Freedom Party), which had grown out of the Irgun, as bearing 'the unmistakable stamp of a Fascist party'.
The letter said that on 9 April terrorist bands attacked Deir Yassin, a 'peaceful village, which was not a military objective', and 'killed most of its inhabitants (240 men, women, and children)'.
Manne reports that Arendt later estimated the Arab 'evacuation' at 500,000.
